subject: Biotechnology
title: Minimal Residual Disease
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Minimal Residual Disease.

hook.text: The tumor is gone on scans — but a few cancer cells may remain. MRD testing finds them before they grow back.

buildup.text: After treatment, ctDNA testing detects residual cancer at levels too low for imaging — molecular evidence of disease.

discovery.text: MRD-positive patients relapse at 10 times the rate of MRD-negative patients — the test predicts the future.

twist.text: MRD can guide de-escalation — if ctDNA is undetectable, patients may safely skip additional chemotherapy.

climax.text: CIRCULATE-Japan is the largest MRD-guided trial — adjusting treatment based on ctDNA status after colon cancer surgery.

punchline.text: Find the last cancer cell — MRD testing catches relapse before it starts.

quiz.question: How can MRD testing help patients avoid unnecessary treatment?
options: It replaces all imaging scans permanently
If ctDNA is undetectable after surgery, patients may safely skip additional chemotherapy
It directly kills remaining cancer cells

details.summary: Minimal residual disease testing detects tiny numbers of remaining cancer cells after treatment using ultra-sensitive molecular methods. Finding as few as one cancer cell among a million normal cells predicts relapse risk and guides decisions about continuing or stopping therapy.
details.whyItMatters: MRD testing transforms cancer follow-up from waiting for visible relapse to proactively detecting microscopic disease. Patients testing MRD-negative after treatment may safely stop therapy, while MRD-positive patients receive intensified treatment
takeaways: MRD detects one cancer cell among a million normal cells after treatment
MRD-negative status predicts excellent long-term outcomes in blood cancers
Testing guides decisions about treatment duration and intensification

faq.question: How is minimal residual disease measured?
faq.answer: Flow cytometry detects cancer cells by surface markers. PCR amplifies tumor-specific gene rearrangements. Next-generation sequencing identifies tumor-specific mutations in blood or bone marrow. Each method detects one cancer cell in 10,000 to 1,000,000 normal cells depending on the technique.

faq.question: In which cancers is MRD testing most useful?
faq.answer: MRD is standard of care in acute lymphoblastic leukemia, chronic myeloid leukemia, and multiple myeloma. It is increasingly used in chronic lymphocytic leukemia and acute myeloid leukemia. Solid tumor MRD using circulating tumor DNA is in development for colorectal, breast, and lung cancers.
